## Week 13 overview {.inverse}

**Session 1: iterators and closures**

- Iterator methods (`.map()`, `.filter()`, `.fold()`, `.collect()`)
- Closures and capture semantics
- Closure traits: `Fn`, `FnMut`, `FnOnce`
- Building data processing pipelines
- Lazy evaluation and allocation choices

**Session 2: smart pointers and error handling**

- Smart pointers: `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, `RefCell<T>`
- Interior mutability patterns
- When to use each smart pointer
- Idiomatic error handling with `Result<T, E>`
- The `?` operator and custom error types

::: {.notes}
This week focuses on iterator composition, closure capture, shared ownership, interior mutability, and explicit error propagation. Evaluate each pattern by the ownership or control-flow problem it solves.
:::

---

## Why idiomatic Rust matters {.inverse}

**What the patterns provide:**

- **Functional style**: Process data without manual loops
- **Flexible ownership**: Build complex data structures safely
- **Explicit errors**: Expected failure categories in return types
- **Iterator composition**: Lazy adaptors that can avoid intermediate collections

**Project examples:**

- [Ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep): Fast search tool using iterators
- [Servo](https://servo.org/): Browser engine with smart pointers
- [Tokio](https://tokio.rs/): Async runtime with Result-based APIs

::: {.notes}
These patterns appear often in Rust code. Learn to recognize their trade-offs and start with the simplest ownership model that satisfies the requirement.
:::

# Session 1: iterators and closures

## The problem: manual iteration {.smaller}

**Traditional loop-based approach:**

```rust
let numbers = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
let mut result = Vec::new();

for num in &numbers {
    if num % 2 == 0 {  // Keep evens
        let squared = num * num;  // Square them
        result.push(squared);
    }
}
// result = [4, 16, 36]
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20numbers%20%3D%20vec%21%5B1%2C%202%2C%203%2C%204%2C%205%2C%206%5D%3B%0Alet%20mut%20result%20%3D%20Vec%3A%3Anew%28%29%3B%0A%0Afor%20num%20in%20%26numbers%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20if%20num%20%25%202%20%3D%3D%200%20%7B%20%20%2F%2F%20Keep%20evens%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20let%20squared%20%3D%20num%20%2A%20num%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Square%20them%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20result.push%28squared%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%7D%0A%2F%2F%20result%20%3D%20%5B4%2C%2016%2C%2036%5D%0A%7D%0A)

**Problems:**

- Mutable state (`result`)
- Multiple steps spread across lines
- Intent buried in implementation
- Error-prone (easy to forget to push, etc.)

::: {.notes}
Ask students: "What if we had 5 different transformations? Code gets messy fast."
:::

---

## Introducing iterators {.smaller}

**Functional approach with iterator chains:**

```rust
let numbers = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

let result: Vec<i32> = numbers
    .iter()
    .filter(|&&n| n % 2 == 0)  // Keep evens
    .map(|&n| n * n)            // Square them
    .collect();

// result = [4, 16, 36]
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20numbers%20%3D%20vec%21%5B1%2C%202%2C%203%2C%204%2C%205%2C%206%5D%3B%0A%0Alet%20result%3A%20Vec%3Ci32%3E%20%3D%20numbers%0A%20%20%20%20.iter%28%29%0A%20%20%20%20.filter%28%7C%26%26n%7C%20n%20%25%202%20%3D%3D%200%29%20%20%2F%2F%20Keep%20evens%0A%20%20%20%20.map%28%7C%26n%7C%20n%20%2A%20n%29%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%20Square%20them%0A%20%20%20%20.collect%28%29%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20result%20%3D%20%5B4%2C%2016%2C%2036%5D%0A%7D%0A)

**Benefits:**

- Declarative: says *what* to do, not *how*
- Composable: chain operations together
- Lazy: only evaluates when needed
- Optimizable: iterator chains can compile to efficient loops, but measure when performance matters

[Iterator trait documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html)

::: {.notes}
Emphasize lazy evaluation - intermediate steps don't create temporary vectors.
:::

---

## Common iterator methods {.smaller}

**Transformation:**

```rust
// map: transform each element
vec![1, 2, 3].iter().map(|x| x * 2)  // [2, 4, 6]

// filter: keep elements matching condition
vec![1, 2, 3, 4].iter().filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0)  // [2, 4]

// filter_map: transform and filter in one step
vec!["1", "two", "3"]
    .iter()
    .filter_map(|s| s.parse::<i32>().ok())  // [1, 3]
```

**Aggregation:**

```rust
// sum: add all elements
vec![1, 2, 3].iter().sum::<i32>()  // 6

// fold: custom aggregation
vec![1, 2, 3].iter().fold(0, |acc, x| acc + x)  // 6

// collect: gather results into a collection
(1..=5).collect::<Vec<i32>>()  // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

[Iterator methods](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#provided-methods)

::: {.notes}
Explain that iterator adaptors are lazy and usually inline well. `collect()` intentionally allocates a collection; inspect optimized output or benchmark before claiming equivalence with a particular loop.
:::

## Practical example: line lengths {.smaller}

**Trim nonempty lines and record their lengths:**

```rust
fn nonempty_line_lengths(text: &str) -> Vec<usize> {
    text.lines()
        .map(str::trim)
        .filter(|line| !line.is_empty())
        .map(str::len)
        .collect()
}
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Afn%20nonempty_line_lengths%28text%3A%20%26str%29%20-%3E%20Vec%3Cusize%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20text.lines%28%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.map%28str%3A%3Atrim%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.filter%28%7Cline%7C%20%21line.is_empty%28%29%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.map%28str%3A%3Alen%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.collect%28%29%0A%7D%0A%7D%0A)

::: {.notes}
Compare this iterator version with a loop using the same requirements. Prefer the version whose data flow the class can explain and test.
:::

## Closures: anonymous functions {.smaller}

**Closures are functions that can capture their environment:**

```rust
// Regular function
fn add_one(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x + 1
}

// Closure (short form)
let add_one = |x: i32| x + 1;

// Closure with type inference (Rust figures it out!)
let add_one = |x| x + 1;

// Use it:
let result = add_one(5);  // 6
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0A%2F%2F%20Regular%20function%0Afn%20add_one%28x%3A%20i32%29%20-%3E%20i32%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20x%20%2B%201%0A%7D%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Closure%20%28short%20form%29%0Alet%20add_one%20%3D%20%7Cx%3A%20i32%7C%20x%20%2B%201%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Closure%20with%20type%20inference%20%28Rust%20figures%20it%20out%21%29%0Alet%20add_one%20%3D%20%7Cx%7C%20x%20%2B%201%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Use%20it%3A%0Alet%20result%20%3D%20add_one%285%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%206%0A%7D%0A)

**Closures can capture variables:**

```rust
let threshold = 10;

// Closure captures 'threshold' from environment
let is_large = |x: i32| x > threshold;

println!("{}", is_large(5));   // false
println!("{}", is_large(15));  // true
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20threshold%20%3D%2010%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Closure%20captures%20%27threshold%27%20from%20environment%0Alet%20is_large%20%3D%20%7Cx%3A%20i32%7C%20x%20%3E%20threshold%3B%0A%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20is_large%285%29%29%3B%20%20%20%2F%2F%20false%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20is_large%2815%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20true%0A%7D%0A)

[Closures in Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch13-01-closures.html)

::: {.notes}
This is where closures shine - they remember their environment!
:::

---

## Closure traits: `Fn`, `FnMut`, and `FnOnce` {.smaller}

**Rust has three closure traits based on how they capture variables:**

**`Fn`** - Borrows immutably:
```rust
let x = 10;
let print_x = || println!("{}", x);  // Borrows x
print_x();  // Can call multiple times
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20x%20%3D%2010%3B%0Alet%20print_x%20%3D%20%7C%7C%20println%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20x%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Borrows%20x%0Aprint_x%28%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Can%20call%20multiple%20times%0A%7D%0A)

**`FnMut`** - Borrows mutably:
```rust
let mut count = 0;
let mut increment = || { count += 1; };  // Mutably borrows count
increment();  // count = 1
increment();  // count = 2
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20mut%20count%20%3D%200%3B%0Alet%20mut%20increment%20%3D%20%7C%7C%20%7B%20count%20%2B%3D%201%3B%20%7D%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Mutably%20borrows%20count%0Aincrement%28%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20count%20%3D%201%0Aincrement%28%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20count%20%3D%202%0A%7D%0A)

**`FnOnce`** - Takes ownership:
```rust
let data = vec![1, 2, 3];
let consume = || drop(data);  // Takes ownership of data
consume();  // data is moved, can't call again
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20data%20%3D%20vec%21%5B1%2C%202%2C%203%5D%3B%0Alet%20consume%20%3D%20%7C%7C%20drop%28data%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Takes%20ownership%20of%20data%0Aconsume%28%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20data%20is%20moved%2C%20can%27t%20call%20again%0A%7D%0A)

[Fn traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/index.html#traits)

::: {.notes}
Most closures are Fn or FnMut. FnOnce is rare but important to understand.
:::

---

## Practical example: captured state {.smaller}

**A closure can update a value from its environment:**

```rust
let mut total = 0;
let mut add_to_total = |amount| {
    total += amount;
    total
};

println!("{}", add_to_total(4));  // 4
println!("{}", add_to_total(7));  // 11
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Alet%20mut%20total%20%3D%200%3B%0Alet%20mut%20add_to_total%20%3D%20%7Camount%7C%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20total%20%2B%3D%20amount%3B%0A%20%20%20%20total%0A%7D%3B%0A%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20add_to_total%284%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%204%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20add_to_total%287%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%2011%0A%7D%0A)

**Key concepts:**

- `FnMut` because the closure mutates captured `total`
- The mutable borrow lasts while the closure may still be used

::: {.notes}
The captured variable gives this closure state that persists between calls.
:::

## Iterator and closure pattern {.smaller}

**Processing collections with closures:**

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Student {
    name: String,
    grade: f64,
}

let students = vec![Student { name: "Alice".to_string(), grade: 92.0 },
    Student { name: "Bob".to_string(), grade: 78.0 },
    Student { name: "Charlie".to_string(), grade: 85.0 },
];

// Find honor roll students (grade >= 80)
let honor_roll: Vec<&str> = students
    .iter()
    .filter(|student| student.grade >= 80.0)
    .map(|student| student.name.as_str())
    .collect();

// honor_roll = ["Alice", "Charlie"]
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%29%5D%0Astruct%20Student%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20name%3A%20String%2C%0A%20%20%20%20grade%3A%20f64%2C%0A%7D%0A%0Alet%20students%20%3D%20vec%21%5BStudent%20%7B%20name%3A%20%22Alice%22.to_string%28%29%2C%20grade%3A%2092.0%20%7D%2C%0A%20%20%20%20Student%20%7B%20name%3A%20%22Bob%22.to_string%28%29%2C%20grade%3A%2078.0%20%7D%2C%0A%20%20%20%20Student%20%7B%20name%3A%20%22Charlie%22.to_string%28%29%2C%20grade%3A%2085.0%20%7D%2C%0A%5D%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Find%20honor%20roll%20students%20%28grade%20%3E%3D%2080%29%0Alet%20honor_roll%3A%20Vec%3C%26str%3E%20%3D%20students%0A%20%20%20%20.iter%28%29%0A%20%20%20%20.filter%28%7Cstudent%7C%20student.grade%20%3E%3D%2080.0%29%0A%20%20%20%20.map%28%7Cstudent%7C%20student.name.as_str%28%29%29%0A%20%20%20%20.collect%28%29%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20honor_roll%20%3D%20%5B%22Alice%22%2C%20%22Charlie%22%5D%0A%7D%0A)

**Transfer**: The same filter-map-collect pipeline appears in many Rust APIs.

::: {.notes}
Trace the item type after each adaptor and confirm which values are borrowed. Avoid presenting a pipeline as automatically clearer than a loop.
:::

# Session 2: smart pointers

## The problem: ownership limitations {.smaller}

**Rust's ownership rules are strict:**

```rust
// ❌ Can't do this - multiple ownership
let data = vec![1, 2, 3];
let owner1 = data;
let owner2 = data;  // ERROR: value moved!
```

```rust
// ❌ Can't do this - recursive types have unknown size
struct Node {
    value: i32,
    next: Node,  // ERROR: infinite size!
}
```

```rust
// ❌ Can't do this - mutation through shared reference
let x = 5;
let y = &x;
*y = 10;  // ERROR: cannot assign through &T
```

**Solution**: Smart pointers!

::: {.notes}
These limitations are by design - they prevent memory bugs. Smart pointers provide safe flexibility.
:::

---

## Smart pointer overview {.smaller}

**Three essential smart pointers:**

| Type | Purpose | Use When |
|------|---------|----------|
| `Box<T>` | Heap allocation | Recursive types, large data |
| `Rc<T>` | Reference counting | Multiple owners (single-threaded) |
| `RefCell<T>` | Interior mutability | Runtime borrowing checks |

**Key insight**: Smart pointers provide additional capabilities while maintaining Rust's safety guarantees.

**Common combinations:**

- `Box<T>` alone: Recursive data structures
- `Rc<T>` alone: Shared read-only data
- `Rc<RefCell<T>>`: Shared mutable data (single-threaded)

[Smart Pointers in Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-00-smart-pointers.html)

::: {.notes}
These types express ownership patterns that ordinary references cannot represent, but they also add complexity.
:::

---

## `Box<T>`: heap allocation {.smaller}

**`Box<T>` stores data on the heap with known size:**

```rust
// Simple heap allocation
let boxed_int = Box::new(5);
println!("{}", *boxed_int);  // 5 (dereference with *)

// Main use case: recursive types
#[derive(Debug)]
enum BinaryTree<T> {
    Empty,
    Node {
        value: T,
        left: Box<BinaryTree<T>>,   // Box enables recursion!
        right: Box<BinaryTree<T>>,
    },
}

// Create a tree
let tree = BinaryTree::Node {
    value: 5,
    left: Box::new(BinaryTree::Empty),
    right: Box::new(BinaryTree::Empty),
};
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0A%2F%2F%20Simple%20heap%20allocation%0Alet%20boxed_int%20%3D%20Box%3A%3Anew%285%29%3B%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20%2Aboxed_int%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%205%20%28dereference%20with%20%2A%29%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Main%20use%20case%3A%20recursive%20types%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%29%5D%0Aenum%20BinaryTree%3CT%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20Empty%2C%0A%20%20%20%20Node%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20value%3A%20T%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20left%3A%20Box%3CBinaryTree%3CT%3E%3E%2C%20%20%20%2F%2F%20Box%20enables%20recursion%21%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20right%3A%20Box%3CBinaryTree%3CT%3E%3E%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%2C%0A%7D%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Create%20a%20tree%0Alet%20tree%20%3D%20BinaryTree%3A%3ANode%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20value%3A%205%2C%0A%20%20%20%20left%3A%20Box%3A%3Anew%28BinaryTree%3A%3AEmpty%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20right%3A%20Box%3A%3Anew%28BinaryTree%3A%3AEmpty%29%2C%0A%7D%3B%0A%7D%0A)

**Why it works**: `Box<T>` has fixed size (just a pointer), even though `T` might be recursive.

[Box documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html)

::: {.notes}
Without Box, compiler can't determine struct size. Box breaks the recursion.
:::

---

## Practical example: binary tree {.smaller}

**Building a binary tree with Box:**

```rust
impl<T> BinaryTree<T> {
    /// Creates a new empty tree
    fn new() -> Self {
        BinaryTree::Empty
    }

    /// Creates a leaf node (no children)
    fn leaf(value: T) -> Self {
        BinaryTree::Node {
            value,
            left: Box::new(BinaryTree::Empty),
            right: Box::new(BinaryTree::Empty),
        }
    }

    /// Creates a node with children
    fn node(value: T, left: BinaryTree<T>, right: BinaryTree<T>) -> Self {
        BinaryTree::Node {
            value,
            left: Box::new(left),
            right: Box::new(right),
        }
    }
}

// Usage:
let tree = BinaryTree::node(
    10,
    BinaryTree::leaf(5),
    BinaryTree::leaf(15),
);
```

::: {.notes}
This pattern appears in compilers, game engines, databases - anywhere trees are needed.
:::

---

## `Rc<T>`: reference counting {.smaller}

**`Rc<T>` enables multiple owners of the same data:**

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct SharedData {
    value: i32,
}

let data = Rc::new(SharedData { value: 42 });
println!("Count: {}", Rc::strong_count(&data));  // 1

// Create additional owners by cloning the Rc
let owner1 = Rc::clone(&data);  // Increments count
let owner2 = Rc::clone(&data);  // Increments count

println!("Count: {}", Rc::strong_count(&data));  // 3
println!("Value: {}", owner1.value);  // 42

// When all Rc's drop, data is freed
drop(owner1);
println!("Count: {}", Rc::strong_count(&data));  // 2
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Arc%3A%3ARc%3B%0A%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%29%5D%0Astruct%20SharedData%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20value%3A%20i32%2C%0A%7D%0A%0Alet%20data%20%3D%20Rc%3A%3Anew%28SharedData%20%7B%20value%3A%2042%20%7D%29%3B%0Aprintln%21%28%22Count%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20Rc%3A%3Astrong_count%28%26data%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%201%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Create%20additional%20owners%20by%20cloning%20the%20Rc%0Alet%20owner1%20%3D%20Rc%3A%3Aclone%28%26data%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Increments%20count%0Alet%20owner2%20%3D%20Rc%3A%3Aclone%28%26data%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20Increments%20count%0A%0Aprintln%21%28%22Count%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20Rc%3A%3Astrong_count%28%26data%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%203%0Aprintln%21%28%22Value%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20owner1.value%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%2042%0A%0A%2F%2F%20When%20all%20Rc%27s%20drop%2C%20data%20is%20freed%0Adrop%28owner1%29%3B%0Aprintln%21%28%22Count%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20Rc%3A%3Astrong_count%28%26data%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%202%0A%7D%0A)

**Important**: `Rc::clone` is cheap - it only increments a counter, doesn't copy data!

[Rc documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/struct.Rc.html)

::: {.notes}
`Rc<T>` is useful for single-threaded structures in which multiple owners share a value, such as some graph representations.
:::

---

## `RefCell<T>`: interior mutability {.smaller}

**`RefCell<T>` allows mutation through shared references (runtime borrow checking):**

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;

let data = RefCell::new(5);

// Borrow immutably
{
    let value = data.borrow();
    println!("{}", *value);  // 5
} // borrow ends here

// Borrow mutably
{
    let mut value = data.borrow_mut();
    *value += 10;
} // borrow ends here

println!("{}", *data.borrow());  // 15
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Acell%3A%3ARefCell%3B%0A%0Alet%20data%20%3D%20RefCell%3A%3Anew%285%29%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Borrow%20immutably%0A%7B%0A%20%20%20%20let%20value%20%3D%20data.borrow%28%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20println%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20%2Avalue%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%205%0A%7D%20%2F%2F%20borrow%20ends%20here%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Borrow%20mutably%0A%7B%0A%20%20%20%20let%20mut%20value%20%3D%20data.borrow_mut%28%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20%2Avalue%20%2B%3D%2010%3B%0A%7D%20%2F%2F%20borrow%20ends%20here%0A%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20%2Adata.borrow%28%29%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%2015%0A%7D%0A)

**Key difference**: Borrows checked at *runtime* instead of compile-time.

**Panic if rules violated**:
```rust
let value1 = data.borrow_mut();
let value2 = data.borrow();  // ❌ PANIC: already borrowed mutably!
```

[RefCell documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html)

::: {.notes}
Use RefCell when you need flexibility that the borrow checker can't statically verify.
:::

---

## Combining `Rc` and `RefCell` {.smaller}

**Pattern: Shared mutable data (single-threaded)**

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::cell::RefCell;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Counter {
    value: i32,
}

let counter = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Counter { value: 0 }));

// Create multiple owners
let counter_ref1 = Rc::clone(&counter);
let counter_ref2 = Rc::clone(&counter);

// All can mutate through RefCell
counter_ref1.borrow_mut().value += 1;
counter_ref2.borrow_mut().value += 1;

println!("{}", counter.borrow().value);  // 2
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Arc%3A%3ARc%3B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Acell%3A%3ARefCell%3B%0A%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%29%5D%0Astruct%20Counter%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20value%3A%20i32%2C%0A%7D%0A%0Alet%20counter%20%3D%20Rc%3A%3Anew%28RefCell%3A%3Anew%28Counter%20%7B%20value%3A%200%20%7D%29%29%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Create%20multiple%20owners%0Alet%20counter_ref1%20%3D%20Rc%3A%3Aclone%28%26counter%29%3B%0Alet%20counter_ref2%20%3D%20Rc%3A%3Aclone%28%26counter%29%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20All%20can%20mutate%20through%20RefCell%0Acounter_ref1.borrow_mut%28%29.value%20%2B%3D%201%3B%0Acounter_ref2.borrow_mut%28%29.value%20%2B%3D%201%3B%0A%0Aprintln%21%28%22%7B%7D%22%2C%20counter.borrow%28%29.value%29%3B%20%20%2F%2F%202%0A%7D%0A)

**Pattern breakdown**:

- `Rc<T>`: Multiple owners
- `RefCell<T>`: Interior mutability
- `Rc<RefCell<T>>`: Multiple owners can all mutate

::: {.notes}
This is the secret sauce for shared mutable state in single-threaded Rust.
:::

---

## When to use each smart pointer {.smaller}

**Decision tree:**

```
Do you need multiple owners?
├─ NO → Use Box<T>
│   └─ For: Recursive types, large data on heap
│
└─ YES → Do you need mutation?
    ├─ NO → Use Rc<T>
    │   └─ For: Shared read-only data
    │
    └─ YES → Use Rc<RefCell<T>>
        └─ For: Shared mutable data (single-threaded)
```

**Multi-threaded variants** (for future study):

- `Arc<T>`: Thread-safe `Rc<T>` (Atomic Reference Counting)
- `Mutex<T>`: Thread-safe `RefCell<T>` (Mutual Exclusion)
- `Arc<Mutex<T>>`: Thread-safe shared mutable data

::: {.notes}
For now, focus on single-threaded ownership. `Arc<T>` and `Mutex<T>` are optional follow-up topics and are not required in Lab 14.
:::

## Idiomatic error handling {.inverse}

**Rust uses `Result<T, E>` for recoverable errors rather than catchable exceptions.**

**What this provides:**

- Errors are explicit in function signatures
- Code must inspect or transform the result to access the success value
- Expected failure categories are visible to callers
- `Result` is an enum whose representation and runtime cost depend on its variants and use

**Two approaches:**

1. **Recoverable errors**: Use `Result<T, E>` (file not found, parse error)
2. **Unrecoverable errors**: Use `panic!` (programming bugs, invariant violations)

::: {.notes}
This is a fundamental mindset shift from exception-based languages.
:::

---

## `Result<T, E>` basics {.smaller}

**`Result` is an enum with two variants:**

```rust
enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),   // Success - contains value
    Err(E),  // Failure - contains error
}

// Example: parsing a network port
fn parse_port(input: &str) -> Result<u16, String> {
    input
        .trim()
        .parse::<u16>()
        .map_err(|_| format!("Invalid port: {input}"))
}

// Usage with match:
match parse_port("8080") {
    Ok(port) => println!("Port: {port}"),
    Err(e) => println!("Error: {}", e),
}

// Or with if let:
if let Ok(port) = parse_port("3000") {
    println!("Port: {port}");
}
```

[Result documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/enum.Result.html)

::: {.notes}
Result forces you to think about errors upfront, not as an afterthought.
:::

---

## The `?` operator: error propagation {.smaller}

**The `?` operator makes error handling ergonomic:**

```rust
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Read};

// Without ?
fn read_file_verbose(path: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let file_result = File::open(path);
    let mut file = match file_result {
        Ok(f) => f,
        Err(e) => return Err(e),  // Early return on error
    };

    let mut contents = String::new();
    match file.read_to_string(&mut contents) {
        Ok(_) => Ok(contents),
        Err(e) => Err(e),
    }
}

// With ? (much cleaner!)
fn read_file(path: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let mut file = File::open(path)?;  // ? propagates error
    let mut contents = String::new();
    file.read_to_string(&mut contents)?;  // ? propagates error
    Ok(contents)
}
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Afs%3A%3AFile%3B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Aio%3A%3A%7Bself%2C%20Read%7D%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Without%20%3F%0Afn%20read_file_verbose%28path%3A%20%26str%29%20-%3E%20io%3A%3AResult%3CString%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20let%20file_result%20%3D%20File%3A%3Aopen%28path%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20let%20mut%20file%20%3D%20match%20file_result%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Ok%28f%29%20%3D%3E%20f%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Err%28e%29%20%3D%3E%20return%20Err%28e%29%2C%20%20%2F%2F%20Early%20return%20on%20error%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%3B%0A%0A%20%20%20%20let%20mut%20contents%20%3D%20String%3A%3Anew%28%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20match%20file.read_to_string%28%26mut%20contents%29%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Ok%28_%29%20%3D%3E%20Ok%28contents%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Err%28e%29%20%3D%3E%20Err%28e%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%7D%0A%0A%2F%2F%20With%20%3F%20%28much%20cleaner%21%29%0Afn%20read_file%28path%3A%20%26str%29%20-%3E%20io%3A%3AResult%3CString%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20let%20mut%20file%20%3D%20File%3A%3Aopen%28path%29%3F%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20%3F%20propagates%20error%0A%20%20%20%20let%20mut%20contents%20%3D%20String%3A%3Anew%28%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20file.read_to_string%28%26mut%20contents%29%3F%3B%20%20%2F%2F%20%3F%20propagates%20error%0A%20%20%20%20Ok%28contents%29%0A%7D%0A%7D%0A)

**`?` means**: "If Ok, unwrap the value. If Err, return the error immediately."

[? operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html#a-shortcut-for-propagating-errors-the--operator)

::: {.notes}
The ? operator is syntactic sugar that makes error handling look clean.
:::

## Custom error types {.smaller}

**Create domain-specific errors:**

```rust
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum ParseError {
    EmptyInput,
    InvalidNumber(String),
    InvalidPercentage(i32),
}

// Implement Display for pretty error messages
impl fmt::Display for ParseError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ParseError::EmptyInput => write!(f, "Input string is empty"),
            ParseError::InvalidNumber(s) => write!(f, "Invalid number: {}", s),
            ParseError::InvalidPercentage(n) => {
                write!(f, "Percentage {n} must be between 0 and 100")
            }
        }
    }
}

// Use custom error type
fn parse_percentage(input: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseError> {
    if input.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err(ParseError::EmptyInput);
    }

    let num: i32 = input.trim().parse()
        .map_err(|_| ParseError::InvalidNumber(input.to_string()))?;

    if !(0..=100).contains(&num) {
        return Err(ParseError::InvalidPercentage(num));
    }

    Ok(num)
}
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Afmt%3B%0A%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%2C%20Clone%29%5D%0Aenum%20ParseError%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20EmptyInput%2C%0A%20%20%20%20InvalidNumber%28String%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20InvalidPercentage%28i32%29%2C%0A%7D%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Implement%20Display%20for%20pretty%20error%20messages%0Aimpl%20fmt%3A%3ADisplay%20for%20ParseError%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20fn%20fmt%28%26self%2C%20f%3A%20%26mut%20fmt%3A%3AFormatter%29%20-%3E%20fmt%3A%3AResult%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20match%20self%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ParseError%3A%3AEmptyInput%20%3D%3E%20write%21%28f%2C%20%22Input%20string%20is%20empty%22%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ParseError%3A%3AInvalidNumber%28s%29%20%3D%3E%20write%21%28f%2C%20%22Invalid%20number%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20s%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ParseError%3A%3AInvalidPercentage%28n%29%20%3D%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20write%21%28f%2C%20%22Percentage%20%7Bn%7D%20must%20be%20between%200%20and%20100%22%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%7D%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Use%20custom%20error%20type%0Afn%20parse_percentage%28input%3A%20%26str%29%20-%3E%20Result%3Ci32%2C%20ParseError%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20if%20input.trim%28%29.is_empty%28%29%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20return%20Err%28ParseError%3A%3AEmptyInput%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%0A%20%20%20%20let%20num%3A%20i32%20%3D%20input.trim%28%29.parse%28%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.map_err%28%7C_%7C%20ParseError%3A%3AInvalidNumber%28input.to_string%28%29%29%29%3F%3B%0A%0A%20%20%20%20if%20%21%280..%3D100%29.contains%28%26num%29%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20return%20Err%28ParseError%3A%3AInvalidPercentage%28num%29%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Ok%28num%29%0A%7D%0A%7D%0A)

::: {.notes}
Custom error variants communicate expected failure categories, but documentation and tests are still needed and unrelated panics may remain.
:::

## Integrative pattern: three concepts {.smaller}

**Combining iterators, smart pointers, and error handling:**

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Config {
    min_length: usize,
    max_length: usize,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum ProcessError {
    LineTooShort(String),
    LineTooLong(String),
}

impl fmt::Display for ProcessError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ProcessError::LineTooShort(line) => write!(f, "Line too short: {}", line),
            ProcessError::LineTooLong(line) => write!(f, "Line too long: {}", line),
        }
    }
}

fn process_lines(
    lines: &[String],
    config: Rc<RefCell<Config>>,  // Smart pointer for shared config
) -> Result<Vec<String>, ProcessError> {  // Result for error handling
    lines
        .iter()  // Iterator
        .map(|line| {
            let cfg = config.borrow();
            let len = line.len();

            if len < cfg.min_length {
                Err(ProcessError::LineTooShort(line.clone()))
            } else if len > cfg.max_length {
                Err(ProcessError::LineTooLong(line.clone()))
            } else {
                Ok(line.to_uppercase())  // Transform on success
            }
        })
        .collect()  // Collect into Result<Vec<_>, _>
}
```

**Try it yourself:** [Run in Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&code=fn%20main%28%29%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Arc%3A%3ARc%3B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Acell%3A%3ARefCell%3B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Afmt%3B%0A%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%2C%20Clone%29%5D%0Astruct%20Config%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20min_length%3A%20usize%2C%0A%20%20%20%20max_length%3A%20usize%2C%0A%7D%0A%0A%23%5Bderive%28Debug%29%5D%0Aenum%20ProcessError%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20LineTooShort%28String%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20LineTooLong%28String%29%2C%0A%7D%0A%0Aimpl%20fmt%3A%3ADisplay%20for%20ProcessError%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20fn%20fmt%28%26self%2C%20f%3A%20%26mut%20fmt%3A%3AFormatter%29%20-%3E%20fmt%3A%3AResult%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20match%20self%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ProcessError%3A%3ALineTooShort%28line%29%20%3D%3E%20write%21%28f%2C%20%22Line%20too%20short%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20line%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ProcessError%3A%3ALineTooLong%28line%29%20%3D%3E%20write%21%28f%2C%20%22Line%20too%20long%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20line%29%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%7D%0A%0Afn%20process_lines%28%0A%20%20%20%20lines%3A%20%26%5BString%5D%2C%0A%20%20%20%20config%3A%20Rc%3CRefCell%3CConfig%3E%3E%2C%20%20%2F%2F%20Smart%20pointer%20for%20shared%20config%0A%29%20-%3E%20Result%3CVec%3CString%3E%2C%20ProcessError%3E%20%7B%20%20%2F%2F%20Result%20for%20error%20handling%0A%20%20%20%20lines%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.iter%28%29%20%20%2F%2F%20Iterator%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.map%28%7Cline%7C%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20let%20cfg%20%3D%20config.borrow%28%29%3B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20let%20len%20%3D%20line.len%28%29%3B%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20if%20len%20%3C%20cfg.min_length%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Err%28ProcessError%3A%3ALineTooShort%28line.clone%28%29%29%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%20else%20if%20len%20%3E%20cfg.max_length%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Err%28ProcessError%3A%3ALineTooLong%28line.clone%28%29%29%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%20else%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Ok%28line.to_uppercase%28%29%29%20%20%2F%2F%20Transform%20on%20success%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%7D%29%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20.collect%28%29%20%20%2F%2F%20Collect%20into%20Result%3CVec%3C_%3E%2C%20_%3E%0A%7D%0A%7D%0A)

::: {.notes}
Summarize the decision points: iterator versus loop, single versus shared ownership, compile-time versus runtime borrow checking, and `Result` propagation versus local handling.
:::

## Where these patterns appear {.inverse .smaller}

**Where you'll use these patterns:**

**Iterators:**

- Data processing pipelines (ETL, analytics)
- Web server request filtering
- Database query building
- JSON/XML parsing

**Smart pointers:**

- Graph databases (Rc for shared nodes)
- Game engines (entity-component systems)
- Compilers (AST with shared subtrees)
- UI frameworks (shared state management)

**Error handling:**

- Library APIs that expose recoverable failure
- File I/O, network requests, parsing
- Database operations
- Command-line tools

**Review prompt**: For each pattern, name the ownership or error-handling constraint that motivates it.

::: {.notes}
Use one primary-source example for each pattern and identify where a simpler owned value, loop, or local error branch would be sufficient.
:::

## Common pitfalls and practices {.smaller}

**Iterators:**

❌ Collecting unnecessarily: `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` then iterate again
✅ Chain operations: `.map().filter().sum()` in one go

❌ Using `clone()` in iterators when reference works
✅ Use references or `Copy` types

**Smart Pointers:**

❌ Using `Rc<RefCell<T>>` when `&mut T` works
✅ Start simple, add smart pointers only when needed

❌ Creating reference cycles with `Rc` (memory leak!)
✅ Use `Weak<T>` for back-references

**Error Handling:**

❌ Using `.unwrap()` everywhere (panics in production!)
✅ Use `?` operator and handle errors properly

❌ String errors: `Err("something failed".to_string())`
✅ Custom error enums with specific variants

::: {.notes}
These mistakes are common in beginners. Avoid them from the start!
:::

---

## Optional advanced topics {.inverse .smaller}

**If you want to go deeper:**

**Custom Iterators:**

- Implement the `Iterator` trait
- Create infinite sequences
- Build adapters like `filter` and `map`

**More Smart Pointers:**

- `Weak<T>`: Non-owning references (break cycles)
- `Cow<T>`: Clone-on-write
- `Pin<T>`: Prevent moves (async/await)

**Error Libraries:**

- [`thiserror`](https://docs.rs/thiserror/): Derive Error trait
- [`anyhow`](https://docs.rs/anyhow/): Convenient error handling

**None of these are required for Lab 13, but great for projects!**

::: {.notes}
These are for students who want to explore beyond the basics.
:::

## Week 13 summary {.inverse}

**What makes Rust code "idiomatic":**

- **Iterators**: Composable data processing
- **Closures**: Functions that can capture their environment
- **Smart pointers**: Optional tools for ownership patterns that references cannot express
- **Error handling**: Explicit, recoverable errors

**Key takeaways:**

- Iterator chains are lazy and often optimize well; collection and algorithm choices still matter
- Smart pointers add capabilities and complexity; start with ordinary ownership and borrowing
- `Result<T, E>` makes errors part of your API
- These patterns appear throughout Rust's standard library and ecosystem

Next week synthesizes these patterns in a tested password generator and validator CLI built with `clap`.
:::
